title: Structure à l'infini des Mg,ν [pages 1 à 90, dont table des matières] : notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
Context: these are notes on the structure at infinity of M_{g,ν}. The boundary strata of the Deligne–Mumford–Knudsen compactification are indexed by the dual graphs of stable curves, so Grothendieck is setting up a combinatorial category of graphs.

On the previous page he encodes a graph G by:
- a vertex set S;
- a set of oriented arcs Ã, with a fixed-point-free involution σ (reversal) and an origin map.
He notes that an ordinary graph morphism is the same as a morphism of fundamental groupoids Π_1(G') → Π_1(G) that sends arcs to arcs. This works because Π_1 of a graph is the free groupoid on its arcs: its objects are S and it is generated by Ã, with σ(a) = a^{-1}.

On this page he generalizes the notion. A 'morphisme de spécialisation' (he first wrote, then struck, 'généralisation') from G' to G'' is a groupoid morphism Π_1(G') → Π_1(G'') sending every arc of G' either to an arc of G'' or to an identity arrow.

Equivalently, call the 'elementary arrows' of Π_1(G') the identities together with the arcs; this set is stable under inversion. The specialization morphisms are then exactly the groupoid morphisms that send elementary arrows to elementary arrows. Because the condition is phrased as 'preserves a distinguished class of arrows', stability under composition is immediate.

The next page makes the definition concrete. Such a morphism is:
- a map S'∐Ã' → S''∐Ã'' that sends S' into S'' and is compatible with σ and with 'origin';
- equivalently, a vertex map f_S, together with a σ-stable subset B̃' ⊂ Ã' and a σ-compatible map B̃' → Ã'';
- with the condition that each collapsed arc has endpoints with the same image.

In modern terms these are graph morphisms that may contract edges: morphisms of reflexive graphs with orientation-reversal involution. When surjective, they are the edge contractions that describe how dual graphs of stable curves behave under specialization in the boundary stratification of M̄_{g,n}. This is the morphism notion of the category of stable graphs used for modular operads and in tropical moduli.
errors: No mathematical error on this page. The definition is correct because Π_1 of a graph is the free groupoid on the arcs, so a groupoid morphism is determined by the images of the arcs and the vertex map.

Direction and naming wobble. Grothendieck hesitates between 'généralisation' and 'spécialisation' (one struck, the other inserted). The previous page also writes 'morphismes de G dans G'' while the groupoid map goes Π_1(G') → Π_1(G), which is a minor directional slip.

As written, the definition does not require surjectivity or that only edges are collapsed. It therefore includes more than pure contractions, e.g. non-surjective maps and maps folding several arcs onto one. This is presumably intentional generality, but it is broader than the specialization maps that actually occur between dual graphs of stable curves.

ideas.what: Morphisms of graphs identified with morphisms of their fundamental (free) groupoids that send arcs to arcs
ideas.modern_name: Fundamental groupoid of a graph as the free groupoid on the graph; Serre-style graphs with an involution

ideas.what: Generalized ('specialization') morphisms of graphs: groupoid morphisms sending elementary arrows (arcs or identities) to elementary arrows, i.e. allowing arcs to be collapsed
ideas.modern_name: Reflexive-graph morphisms / edge contractions; morphisms in the category of stable graphs
ideas.usually_credited_to: Graph contractions are classical. For moduli of curves: Deligne–Mumford–Knudsen boundary stratification; Getzler–Kapranov (modular operads, 1998); Abramovich–Caporaso–Payne (tropical moduli)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a clean, slightly elegant formulation: edge-contracting graph maps characterized as groupoid maps preserving 'elementary arrows'. It is a standard notion, and a specialist would find nothing new beyond its being an early, unpublished setup of the stable-graph category by Grothendieck.
transcription_corrections: Graph letters: the page should probably read G' and G'' (consistent with the previous page's G, G' and the next page's G', G''), not C' and C^♯.
The final line is very uncertain. It is probably 'la donnée d'un morphisme de généralisation [de] G', G'' est définie...' (continued on the next page as 'par une application (44)').
